name: Gary K. Michelson
title: Co-founder and Board Chair, California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy; Initiative Proponent, Proposition 38 (2026)
background: Michelson was born January 14, 1949, in Philadelphia, one of four brothers raised by his mother and grandmother; his grandmother's struggles with syringomyelia, a spinal-cord disorder, are described by his own foundation as the source of his early interest in spinal disease. He graduated from Central High School of Philadelphia in 1966, attended Temple University and Hahnemann Medical College of Drexel University, completed an orthopedic surgery residency at Hahnemann Medical Hospital in 1979, and completed a spinal-surgery fellowship through a joint program of St. Luke's Medical Center, Baylor College of Medicine, and the University of Texas. (Source: Wikipedia, Gary Michelson.)

Michelson practiced as a spinal surgeon for more than 25 years, developing implants, instruments, and surgical techniques aimed at reducing blood loss and incision size, and retired from private practice in 2001 to focus on philanthropy. He holds sole credit on more than 950 issued or pending patents worldwide related to spinal-disorder treatment. In 2005 he sold a large portfolio of his spine-related patents to Medtronic for $1.35 billion, after a legal fight in which he successfully defended against a Medtronic lawsuit; that litigation established a legal precedent, decided in 2004, governing who bears the cost of pretrial discovery of electronic evidence. The Medtronic sale put him on the Forbes 400 list. (Source: Wikipedia, Gary Michelson.)

Michelson has since built a network of philanthropic foundations. The Michelson Medical Research Foundation, renamed from an original 1995 charitable foundation, funds initiatives including the USC Michelson Center for Convergent Bioscience and the Institute for Protein Design at the University of Washington; in 2024 the Michelsons gave $120 million to launch the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy on UCLA-owned research park land, of which Michelson is co-founder and board chair. The Michelson Found Animals Foundation, also founded in 2005, created the first free national pet-microchipping registry after Hurricane Katrina and has funded research toward non-surgical spay/neuter methods for cats and dogs. Other Michelson-founded entities include the Michelson Center for Public Policy, the Michelson 20MM Foundation (funding free online college textbooks), the Michelson Institute for Intellectual Property, and the Michelson Neglected Disease Initiative, run with the Sabin Vaccine Institute. Since 2017 Michelson-backed advocacy has been credited with advancing several California bills on animal welfare, including a law requiring pet shops to source animals from local shelters and a ban on animal testing for cosmetics, as well as the federal FDA Modernization Act 2.0. Michelson was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2011 and the National Academy of Inventors in 2014. (Source: Wikipedia, Gary Michelson.)

Michelson personally filed Proposition 38 with the California Attorney General on October 28, 2025. The measure authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, with half the funds required by statute to go to a single nonprofit research institute meeting a specific set of criteria: prior 501(c)(3) status, UCLA-level hospital patient volume, at least 200,000 square feet of research space, at least $250 million in philanthropic commitments already raised, and two separate $50 million commitments to named vaccine and microbiome research programs. A CalMatters investigation, cited in this voter guide's analysis of the measure, found those criteria match only one entity in the state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, the nonprofit Michelson co-founded and chairs, whose reported philanthropic commitments, planned facility size, and Michelson-funded vaccine and microbiome programs align with the statutory thresholds. Michelson and his affiliated Michelson Center for Public Policy are the Yes on 38 campaign's largest funders. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and opposing ballot-argument author Robert M. Kaplan, a former NIH associate director, have both characterized the eligibility criteria as effectively self-dealing; the Yes on 38 campaign disputes that characterization and says the criteria exist to ensure a scientifically credible, operationally ready recipient. (Source: content/measures/ca-prop-38-2026.json in this voter guide, whose sourcing includes CalMatters investigative reporting and the Legislative Analyst's Office analysis of Proposition 38.)
